title: Restaurant covers forecast
about: A nine-worker organization with two cofounders: a CTO leading a Data Scientist, Backend, Frontend, DevOps and QA, and a Chief Product Officer leading a Project Manager and a Designer. builds a 14-day covers forecast and prep plan for a restaurant kitchen: seven documents, one product rule for the founder, a forecast the platform backtests (the first method fails and is reworked), the store, the app, acceptance tests, a merge and a deploy by DevOps.
note: Prepared script for demo mode. Every word a worker says in demo mode comes from this file, and the product shows that. Code in files/ is real and is tested, backtested and deployed for real.
messy: I run a busy restaurant and every week we either over-prep and bin food or run short on a Saturday. I want to know how many covers to expect each day for the next two weeks, and how much to prep, on a simple page the kitchen can check. It has to run on the office computer, and no customer personal data.

objective.product: Covers forecast and prep plan for the kitchen
objective.target_customer: The head chef and the floor manager of one restaurant
objective.primary_outcome: Expected covers for each of the next 14 days, with a prep plan for each day
objective.business_outcome: Less food thrown away and fewer short-staffed nights
objective.success_criteria: The kitchen sees a 14-day covers forecast that beats last week's numbers, with a prep plan for each day
objective.constraints: Runs on the office computer; no customer personal data
objective.priorities: Forecast accuracy first, then the prep plan page

outcomes: The kitchen preps for the covers it will actually serve
Busy days are staffed in advance

requirements.text: The head chef and floor manager of one restaurant see expected covers for each of the next 14 days.
requirements.verification: Brief and spec name the users and the horizon

requirements.text: The forecast is computed from the daily covers history the restaurant records, and new days can be added.
The forecast beats last week's numbers (the same weekday a week before) on held-out days.
The covers history is kept in one JSON file; bad rows are refused.
One page shows each day's forecast and prep number, weekends marked.
The prep margin over the forecast is a business rule decided by the founder.
Standard library only, one process on the office computer, no customer personal data.
requirements.verification: Architecture review and the delivery contract

requirements.text: Acceptance checks are automated and rerun on every change.
Runs as one process with a health check and a rollback path.
requirements.verification: Health check and smoke test on the live URL

cofounders.why: Owns the architecture, the engineering team, and reviews and merges the release.
Owns the business brief and the prep margin, a trade-off between waste and running out.

CTO.summary: A data scientist owns the method and its evidence, engineers the store and the page, QA the acceptance tests, and DevOps ships it.

roles.why: Owns the forecasting method, its evaluation and forecast.py.
Builds the app and the kitchen's page.
Writes the test plan and the automated acceptance tests.
Writes the runbook and proposes and runs the deploy on the office computer.

CPO.summary: A Project Manager writes the spec and coordinates; a Designer designs the one screen the kitchen reads every morning.

roles.why: Writes the spec and the acceptance checks, assigns the work and clears Blockers.
Designs the one screen the kitchen reads every morning.

t_03.problem: The prep plan needs a margin over the forecast, and nothing says how much. Too little and a busy night runs short; too much and food is thrown away.
t_03.recommendation: Prep for the forecast plus 10 percent, rounded up to whole covers. Review it after four weeks of real numbers.
t_03.what_would_change_this: Four weeks of real covers showing the forecast error is well above or below 10 percent.

t_05.acceptance_check: Method and its evaluation against the baseline.

t_07.summary: Forecast written: the recent average for every day ahead, with tests.
Reworked from the backtest: each day is the average of the same weekday over the last four weeks, as method.md says.
